opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it comes down to what I feel I can trust. When people make those beautiful two-dimensional pictures of loss landscapes, with valleys and mountains, it's very tempting to read a lot into them. But you're taking a space with millions or billions of dimensions and projecting it down onto a plane chosen somewhat arbitrarily, often along random directions. Random directions in very high-dimensional space behave in strange ways, and our intuitions from three-dimensional terrain just don't carry over. So I worry those pictures tell us more about our visualization choices than about the network.

A one-dimensional slice, especially a linear interpolation between two specific points you care about, asks a much more precise question. If I train two networks from the same starting point with different SGD noise, or take two checkpoints from the same run, and walk in a straight line between them, does the loss go up? That's a concrete, falsifiable question with a crisp answer. Either there's a barrier or there isn't. That's the heart of the linear mode connectivity work: we weren't trying to map the whole landscape, just testing one specific property in a way where I'd believe the result.

It's also humbling. One-dimensional slices don't pretend to be the full story. They tell you something true about a very particular path, and you have to be careful about generalizing. But I'd rather have a small fact I'm confident in than a big picture I'm not sure is real. And it turns out those small facts, like the point in training when networks become stable to SGD noise, can be surprisingly informative about things like lottery tickets and pruning. So it's partly scientific taste: start with the simplest measurement that can actually surprise you, and build up from there.

r001.rationale: The response describes a line between networks trained from the same starting point with different SGD noise, but it does not specify different random seeds or say they occupy the same convex region.

r002.rationale: It says a landscape with millions or billions of dimensions is projected onto an arbitrarily chosen plane and warns that the pictures may reflect visualization choices more than the network, conveying that the projection loses landscape information.

r003.rationale: It says one-dimensional slices tell something true about a particular path while not representing the full story, directly limiting their claim to the subset examined.

r004.rationale: It explains that interpolating between specific network points makes the slice a precise, falsifiable test, giving the connection between the networks its meaning.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's because the full loss landscape is something I can't look at. A network like ResNet-50 has tens of millions of parameters, so the landscape lives in a space with tens of millions of dimensions. There's no way to visualize that, and I think any time someone shows you a pretty 3D picture of a loss landscape, you should be a little suspicious about what got thrown away to make it.

So the question becomes: what's the smallest, most honest thing I can measure? And a one-dimensional slice is about as honest as it gets. You pick two points in weight space that you actually care about, say the weights at initialization and the weights at the end of training, or two networks trained from the same starting point with different data orders. Then you draw a straight line between them and evaluate the loss at every point along that line. That's it. There's no projection, no dimensionality reduction, no choice of random directions that might or might not be representative. You're asking a concrete question: if I interpolate between these two solutions, does the loss stay low, or does it spike?

And that question turns out to be surprisingly informative. In the lottery ticket work, and then more directly in the linear mode connectivity work with Gintare Dziugaite, Daniel Roy, and Michael Carbin, we found that whether two trained networks are linearly connected without a barrier tells you something about the stability of training. Early in training, if you make two copies of a network and train them with different SGD noise, they end up in places with a big loss barrier between them. A little later, past some point, they land in the same basin and the line between them is flat. That's a real, measurable phenomenon, and it correlates with when the lottery ticket subnetworks start to work. I wouldn't have found that by trying to render the whole landscape.

The other thing I'd say is that the slice tells you only what it tells you. If I see a barrier, I know those two points are not connected along that line. I don't know whether there's a curved path around it, and in fact there usually is. If I see no barrier, I know something fairly strong about that pair. I like that the claims stay small, because the field has a history of overclaiming from visualizations. One dimension keeps me honest, and it's cheap enough that I can run it across hundreds of checkpoints and seeds and actually get statistics rather than one anecdotal picture.

r001.rationale: It describes comparing loss along the line between two networks started from the same point and trained with different data orders or SGD noise, then uses whether they share a basin to assess training stability.

r002.rationale: It says low-dimensional visualizations discard information from the full high-dimensional landscape and specifically warns about what is thrown away in 3D pictures.

r003.rationale: It presents a one-dimensional slice as a direct measurement along a specific line and limits conclusions to what happens on that line.

r004.rationale: It explains that the slice connects two chosen weight configurations and that the loss along this line reveals whether those solutions are separated by a barrier.

astra-6.text:
Well, the loss landscape of a neural network lives in an incredibly high-dimensional space—one dimension for every parameter—and we can’t really visualize that. But we can take two points in that space, draw a straight line between them, and ask what happens to the loss as we move along that line. Now we have something we can plot and reason about.

And that lets us ask a concrete question: are these two solutions separated by a barrier along that path, or can we interpolate between them without the loss going up? It’s a very limited view of the landscape, but that’s also the appeal. Rather than trying to characterize everything, we can make a precise observation and see what it tells us about training.

r001.rationale: It discusses a line between two points, but does not identify networks trained with different random seeds from a shared checkpoint or investigate whether they occupy the same convex region.

r002.rationale: It says a line plot is a “very limited view” of an incredibly high-dimensional landscape and that it does not characterize everything, communicating that the visualization omits information.

r003.rationale: It describes observing loss along a line, but does not say the slice faithfully represents the landscape within that subset.

r004.rationale: It connects two points with a straight line and explains that examining loss along that connection enables concrete comparisons such as whether a barrier separates the solutions.

sol-6.1.text:
The honest answer is that I can draw them. A neural network’s loss landscape has millions of dimensions, and I don’t have a good way to visualize that. But if I pick two points—say, the weights at initialization and the weights at the end of training—and look at the loss along the line between them, I can plot it and start asking concrete questions.

Of course, that’s a very limited view. A one-dimensional slice can miss all sorts of interesting structure, and the direction you choose matters. But I like starting with something simple that I can actually inspect, then seeing how far that gets us.

r001.rationale: It describes a line from initialization to the end of training, not comparisons between networks trained with different random seeds from a shared checkpoint.

r002.rationale: It says a one-dimensional slice is a limited view that can miss interesting structure, communicating that the visualization loses information about the full landscape.

r003.rationale: It says the line can be plotted and inspected, but does not clearly state that the slice faithfully represents the landscape within the subset it examines.

r004.rationale: It describes drawing a line between two weight points, but does not identify the connection between two networks as what makes the slices meaningful.
